/.title: Work-from-home experiment in a call centre (Ctrip, QJE 2015)
/.problem: Can we predict what four days a week at home does to call-centre output and quits?
/.situation: In December 2010 Ctrip let 131 of 249 volunteer call-centre employees in Shanghai work from home four days a week for nine months; the other 118 stayed in the office. Who went home was decided by an even or odd birthday, so the two groups are directly comparable.
/.data_used: The authors' replication files: a weekly performance panel for every call-centre employee from January 2010 (calls answered and an overall performance score), each participant's pre-experiment characteristics (commute, family, tenure, pay), and who quit by the end of the experiment.
/.protocol_line: Simulation predictions use each employee's 2010 record and assumptions from research published before the experiment's results. Outcomes after 6 December 2010 are used only to check accuracy.
/.intro: Simulates the 249 volunteers of Ctrip's 2010-11 work-from-home experiment as digital twins over the nine months: half work from home four days a week, half stay in the office. Each twin carries its own 2010 call volume and performance level, and its weekly output and quit risk respond to home working through assumptions taken from earlier research. The prediction is scored against the randomized experiment; the alternative asks what two home days a week would have done, the arrangement Trip.com tested a decade later.
/.world: 249 call-centre employees in Shanghai over 38 weeks (6 Dec 2010 to 19 Aug 2011). 131 were randomly sent home four days a week. Every participant is a digital twin built from their own 2010 weekly record and characteristics; outcomes are weekly calls answered, the overall performance score and quits, scored at the group level against the experiment.
/.source: manifests/sources.json (Bloom, Liang, Roberts & Ying 2015 replication files; Harvard Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/PZQOB1, CC0)

takeaways: Effect of working at home on weekly calls answered: the simulation predicted +7.6%; the experiment measured +13.4%. That is further from the actual than the best other prediction (Earlier research, +16.6%).
Effect of working at home on quits: the simulation predicted -1.3 pp; the experiment measured -18.7 pp. That is further from the actual than the best other prediction (Earlier research, -1.6 pp).

Effect of working at home on the overall performance score: the simulation predicted +0.23 SD; the experiment measured +0.20 SD. That is closer than the best other prediction (Earlier research, +0.36 SD).
Weekly calls per order taker, home group: simulation 492.6 calls, actual 449.5 calls, accuracy 90.4%.
Quit by the end of the experiment, home group: simulation +16.2%, actual +16.0%, accuracy 98.9%.
Alternative (two home days): the simulated effect on calls changes from +7.9% to +5.2%, and on quits from -1.0 pp to -0.4 pp (matching runs).

d_perf.source: Telecommuting and supervisor-rated or objective job performance: mean r = .18, d = .36, 95% CI for r .09 to .26 (k = 4, n = 484); Gajendran & Harrison (2007), 'The good, the bad, and the unknown about telecommuting', Journal of Applied Psychology 92(6), 1524-1541, Table 1. The range converts the CI for r to d (2r / sqrt(1 - r^2)). Applied as a shift of d between-person standard deviations of each measure.

d_turnover_intent.source: Telecommuting and turnover intent: mean r = -.08, d = -.17, 95% CI for r -.11 to -.06 (k = 9, n = 7,580); Gajendran & Harrison (2007), Table 1. Range converts the CI to d.

rho_intent_quit.source: Quit intentions predict actual turnover: corrected r = .38 (uncorrected .35, second correction .45; k = 71, N = 63,232); Griffeth, Hom & Gaertner (2000), 'A meta-analysis of antecedents and correlates of employee turnover', Journal of Management 26(3), 463-488. Used as the shift in the latent quit liability per SD of intent.

rho_tenure_quit.source: Organisational tenure and turnover: r = -.20 (corrected -.20 and -.23; 1995 estimate -.17); Griffeth, Hom & Gaertner (2000). Latent quit liability per SD of tenure within the twins.

rho_age_quit.source: Age and turnover: r = -.09 (corrected -.09 and -.11; 1995 estimate -.12); Griffeth, Hom & Gaertner (2000). Latent quit liability per SD of age within the twins.

intensity_share_2d.source: Effect of two home days relative to four (used only by the two-day alternative). Gajendran & Harrison (2007), Table 3: telecommuting lowered work-family conflict at high intensity (2.5 or more days, r = -.16) about three times as much as at low intensity (r = -.05), while its link with perceived autonomy did not differ by intensity (r = .16 vs .15). The range spans those two ratios; the central value is their midpoint.
